source: Gentner (1983) Structure-mapping: a theoretical framework for analogy
finding: Founding claim: analogy maps relations between objects, not object attributes, from base to target. Which relations are mapped is set by systematicity: relations that sit under higher-order relations (cause, implies) that can themselves be mapped. The rules use only the syntax of the representation, not domain content. The same framework separates analogy, literal similarity and abstraction.
numbers: No experiment numbers in the pages I could read. Summary section only.
quote: The structure-mapping theory describes the implicit interpretation rules of analogy.
limits: Scanned PDF: only the last pages (p.168-170 summary and discussion) came out as readable text; the first pages were OCR noise. The core tables and the flowing-waters data are not verified from this copy.
agent_relevance: The theory depends only on form (types and nesting), so a typed mapping scored by code is faithful to it: no domain knowledge is needed to score.

source: Gentner (1983) Structure-mapping: a theoretical framework for analogy
finding: Predicted access asymmetry: when base and target overlap in many object attributes, little is learned from the match; sparse overlap is easier to analyse. Analogies are less likely to be noticed than literal matches because they need access by relations, not objects. Once found, they are more useful for deriving general principles. A general law needs a further step: build a new relational structure with objects stripped of specific attributes.
numbers: Qualitative prediction, no figures.
limits: Same scanned-copy limit as a01. The access side was later tested (Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus 1993; see subfield 03).
agent_relevance: Supports a design where far analogues are used at impasses and the mapping is then abstracted into a schema, not reused raw.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: SME takes a base and a target description and builds all structurally consistent mappings (called gmaps) without backtracking. Each gmap has entity and predicate pairings, candidate inferences (base statements connected to the match but missing in the target) and a structural evaluation score (SES). Two hard constraints: one-to-one pairing, and parallel connectivity (if two statements match, their arguments must match too).
numbers: Water-flow/heat-flow example: best gmap maps beaker to coffee, vial to ice cube, water to heat, pipe to bar, pressure to temperature; candidate inference is that the temperature difference causes the heat flow. Isolated relations such as GREATER-THAN(DIAMETER(beaker), DIAMETER(vial)) are dropped.
limits: Inputs are hand-built predicate descriptions. Mapping ignores all non-structural factors (relevance, goals) by design.
agent_relevance: This is the exact shape of an O7 typed mapping: pairings, a set of carried-over inferences, and a code-computed score. The 1:1 and parallel-connectivity constraints can be checked by plain code.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: Systematicity is implemented locally by trickle-down evidence. Each match hypothesis gets local evidence (e.g. 0.5 if functors are the same). A rule then passes 80% of a match's belief to the matches of its arguments. So entity pairings inside a large matched structure score far above isolated ones. The gmap's SES is the sum of the evidence of its match hypotheses.
numbers: Propagation weight 0.8 of parent belief to children; same-functor local evidence 0.5. Early versions combined gmap evidence with Dempster's rule (roundoff problems, and scores not comparable across base domains), so the final form is a plain sum.
quote: propagating 80% of a match hypothesis' belief to its offspring
limits: Weights were chosen by the authors, not fitted to data. Plain summation 'sufficed for most examples' per the paper.
agent_relevance: A small scoring function (sum with top-down discount) can rank candidate mappings. It needs no model call. The constants are free parameters to test.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: Worked science example. For solar system to Rutherford atom SME builds 3 gmaps. Best (SES 6.03) pairs nucleus with sun and electron with planet, via the mass inequality, and yields the standard inference that mass difference plus attraction causes the revolution. A second gmap maps temperature difference onto mass difference (SES 4.04); a third, spurious, swaps masses (SES 1.87).
numbers: SES 6.03 vs 4.04 vs 1.87. The second is low because temperature has no systematic relational structure on the atom side, and because different functions get less local evidence.
limits: One simplified hand-coded pair of descriptions. Ranking agrees with the textbook reading, but there is no human data in this paper.
agent_relevance: Shows the failure a code check must catch: right entities but a wrong relation mapping gets a lower score because it lacks supporting structure.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: SME is a family of matchers: one engine with different rule sets. Analogy maps only relations (attributes ignored unless part of higher-order structure). Literal similarity maps relations and object attributes. Mere appearance maps mainly attributes. A fourth type, abstraction, treats base entities as variables.
numbers: Examples given: 'Kool-Aid is like juice' (literal), 'The road is like a silver ribbon' (mere appearance). Over 40 examples run at the time of writing.
limits: The three rule sets were designed by hand. The paper cites psychology showing different comparison types behave differently, but the typing is a theoretical choice.
agent_relevance: The type of comparison (analogy vs surface) is a parameter the agent can set per use: relation-only for transfer, attribute-inclusive for near cases.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: Complexity analysis and limits. Most steps are polynomial (about linear in match hypotheses); the final merge of kernels is O(N!) in the worst case. Run times are seconds on typical examples, but flat, unstructured descriptions blow up: a baseball analogy could not be run in hours; one PHINEAS problem took 53 minutes and fell to 34 seconds when more systematic structure was added.
numbers: 53 minutes down to 34 seconds with better structure. 70-80% of run time was in the belief-maintenance system that computes scores.
limits: 1989 hardware (Symbolics 3640). Later work replaced the exhaustive merge with a greedy one (see a20).
agent_relevance: Representation quality drives cost. If the agent writes flat fact lists, mapping search will be expensive and noisy; nested relational form is cheaper and scores better.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The Structure-Mapping Engine: algorithm and examples
finding: The paper argues for a modular matcher against Holyoak's purely pragmatic account: without structural consistency the search space explodes; relevance cannot be required because analogy is also used to explain and to notice irrelevant commonalities; and access is driven by surface similarity, not relevance. It also states a limit: SME ignores non-structural factors.
numbers: Pragmatic account then had 2 published running examples vs 40+ for SME (authors' count).
limits: Authors are partisans in the SME vs ACME debate; the claim about the pragmatic account is theirs, not a test.
agent_relevance: Keep the structural scorer separate from the relevance judgement: score structure by code, judge usefulness to the goal elsewhere.

source: Gentner and Toupin (1986) Systematicity and surface similarity in the development of analogy
finding: Children acted out stories with toy characters, then re-acted them with new characters. Two factors: systematicity (stories with explicit causal structure vs without) and transparency of object correspondences (similar characters, different characters, cross-mapped where look-alikes play different roles). Transparency hurt both ages. Systematicity helped only 8-10 year olds, and only in the hardest, cross-mapped condition.
numbers: About 72 children (df 68), ages 5-7 and 8-10. 2x2x3 ANOVA: Age F(1,68)=14.93, Systematicity F(1,68)=6.28 p<.05, Mapping F(2,136)=29.01, Systematicity x Mapping F(2,136)=3.89 p<.05. Older group: t(34)=2.48 p<.01 for systematic over nonsystematic; younger: t(34)=1.08 not significant.
limits: The paper notes no significant Age x Systematicity interaction, so the developmental difference is tentative. Authors give a knowledge account too (younger children may lack the higher-order relations). Adult data only preliminary.
agent_relevance: Systematic structure matters most when surface cues mislead. This is the case for O7: lean on the structure check most when the analogue looks similar but is cross-mapped.

source: Gentner and Toupin (1986) Systematicity and surface similarity in the development of analogy
finding: Control against a pure memory account: children did equally well on the original enactments in all conditions, and the systematicity effect appeared only in the hardest mapping condition, so it is not an across-the-board memory advantage for organised stories.
numbers: Original-story enactment uniformly good; systematicity significant only in the cross-mapped condition within the older group.
limits: Argument from design, not a separate memory test.
agent_relevance: Cross-mapped cases are where structure scoring pays off; on easy matches it adds little.

source: Clement and Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 1. Adults read base and target passages (novel planets and organisms). Each target held two equally plausible key facts: one linked to a causal system that matched the base (shared-system), one linked to a different causal system. Told the passages were analogous, subjects rated the shared-system fact as better support for the analogy; target-only controls did not.
numbers: N=48 undergraduates. Ratings (1-7): shared-system 6.28 vs different-system 4.89; controls 5.22 vs 5.31. Interaction F'(1,44)=13.99 p<.001. Choice task: mean shared-system picks out of 4 was 3.17 (analogy) vs 2.0 (controls), F(1,44)=18.43 p<.001; per passage 67-92% vs 42-54%; significant on 3 of 4 passages.
quote: The analogy subjects chose the shared-system fact 67% to 92% of the time
limits: One passage was weak. Passages were written by the authors and subjects could re-read the texts. Justifications showed some picked the right fact without being able to say why.
agent_relevance: Direct human evidence that connection to a matched causal chain, not the fact alone, decides which commonalities count. Supports a rule: weight a correspondence by the matched structure it sits in.

source: Clement and Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 2: with the two key facts removed from the target, subjects asked to predict new facts mostly predicted the shared-system fact. So candidate inferences are chosen by systematicity too, not only matches.
numbers: N=32 undergraduates (16 per condition). Free prediction: .53 of analogy responses were the shared-system fact vs .12 the different-system fact. Forced choice: analogy 87% and 69% on two passages vs controls 44% and 25% (p<.05 one-tailed); on the other two passages analogy 62% and 75% vs controls 69% and 44%, not significant.
limits: Half the passages did not separate from controls in the choice task. One passage looked biased toward the systematic fact (controls 69%).
agent_relevance: Inferences carried from an analogue should be those hanging off matched structure. A code rule can reject inferences with no matched support.

source: Clement and Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Experiment 3: the effect held when the base passage was memorised and not on view, though it was smaller.
numbers: N=48. Mean (shared-system minus different-system predictions over 3 passages): analogy .92 vs target-only .13, F(1,44)=5.15 p<.05.
limits: Smaller and less certain (p<.05 only) than Exp 1; passage differences noted by the authors.
agent_relevance: The preference does not depend on having both texts in view, which is the situation of an agent recalling an analogue.

source: Markman and Gentner (1993) one-shot mapping with cross-mapped pictures, as reported in Gentner and Kurtz (2006)
finding: With cross-mapped picture pairs (a man repairing a robot vs a robot repairing a car), people asked to map the cross-mapped object mostly chose the look-alike. If they first rated the similarity of the scenes, they switched to the relational match. Comparing seems to trigger structural alignment.
numbers: Control group chose the object match about 65% of the time; after a similarity rating about 30% object and 70% relational.
limits: Second-hand figures from Gentner and Kurtz's review, not read in the original (Markman and Gentner 1993, Cognitive Psychology 25). Object matches were still chosen about 30% after comparison.
agent_relevance: Asking for an explicit comparison first moves the answer toward structure. This suggests a prompt step that lists matching relations before mapping objects.

source: Markman and Gentner (1993) Splitting the differences: a structural alignment view of similarity
finding: Alignable differences (differences tied to a shared structure, e.g. both have wheels, one has two, one four) are listed more than nonalignable ones, and track the number of commonalities. Similar pairs yield more commonalities and more alignable differences; dissimilar pairs more nonalignable ones. A feature-count model does not predict this.
numbers: Exp 1 (word pairs): rated similarity high 7.4 vs low 1.8; commonalities 6.63 vs 2.78; alignable differences 4.14 vs 3.32; nonalignable 0.62 vs 2.07; commonalities vs alignable r(38)=.45, vs nonalignable r(38)=-.58. Exp 2: alignable 2.41 vs nonalignable 0.98 per pair. Of 67 related commonality-difference pairs (6/12 criterion), 61 (91%) were a commonality with an alignable difference.
limits: Scoring by one rater who knew the hypothesis (naive rater checked 20%: 92% agreement). Word pairs only; Exp 1 used extreme similarity levels so correlations may be inflated (the authors say so).
agent_relevance: The useful differences between a case and its analogue are the ones tied to the mapping. A difference report should list alignable differences first, since they bear on whether the transferred plan still fits.

source: Gentner and Markman (1994, as reported in Gentner and Markman 1997) difference listing for similar vs dissimilar word pairs
finding: People find it easier to list differences for similar pairs than for dissimilar pairs, against a feature-intersection model. The gap is concentrated in alignable differences. The 1993 Exp 2 repeated it with groups seeing only one kind of pair, so it is not a time-allocation artefact.
numbers: 40 word pairs, 5 minutes, one difference each. Similar pairs M=11.4 vs dissimilar M=5.9 pairs completed; alignable differences M=9.0 vs 3.9. 1993 Exp 2 (N=48): 18.42 vs 13.63 items, t(46)=2.75.
limits: Word-pair paradigm, adult students. Numbers here from a review article.
agent_relevance: A within-paper replication of the effect with a control for time spent.

source: Gentner and Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity (American Psychologist)
finding: Review stating the constraints of alignment: one-to-one mapping, parallel connectivity, systematicity, and carryover of candidate inferences. Shows the same process in similarity, so commonalities and differences both depend on the alignment. Notes retrieval is a different story: memory access favours surface similarity.
numbers: Clement and Gentner result cited: people predicted the key fact tied to the matching causal antecedent more than twice as often as the other. Gentner et al. (1993): retrieval rises with surface similarity, while rated soundness rises with shared higher-order structure. Under 700-1000 ms deadlines people used local matches, even cross-mapped; at longer deadlines relational matches dominated.
limits: Review of the authors' own programme. The 'but see Hammond, Seifert, Gray 1991' caveat on surface-driven transfer is cited but not described.
agent_relevance: The two-stage view fits the agent: cheap broad retrieval, then a structural mapping check. The early-vs-late result warns that a fast first pass will rely on surface matches.

source: Gentner and Kurtz (2006) Relations, objects, and the composition of analogies
finding: Three studies varied object match and relation match in sentence pairs and asked whether the pair was an analogy. Relation match dominated acceptance. Changing a noun rarely broke the analogy; changing the verb often did. Related but non-identical relations were accepted, but slower, which supports re-representation. Similarity ratings gave objects more weight than analogy ratings did.
numbers: Exp 1 match type F(1,20)=73.34, semantic distance F(2,20)=38.79, interaction F(2,20)=31.13 (all p<.001). Exp 2 acceptance: verb change .96 (synonym) vs .60 (near) vs .14 (far); noun change .98, .97, .86. Filler pairs accepted .05.
limits: Sentence pairs, not full structures. The authors note earlier work confounded relation count and depth with match type; this study equates them better but is still a lab task. SME's strict identity rule is too strict for language: near relations pass.
agent_relevance: Allow near-synonym relations in a mapping, but flag those mapped pairs as needing a repair step and more checking.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett, Gentner (2017) Extending SME to handle large-scale cognitive modeling
finding: Current SME (version 4) states match rules as: predicates match if identical, or if they are functions and matching them allows a larger relational structure to match (tiered identicality). It no longer has separate rule sets for analogy and similarity; it uses overall similarity and seeks maximal structural consistency. Trickle-down structural evaluation is retained.
numbers: Output limit: mappings must score within 20% of the best (ratio 0.8). Up to about three mappings are kept.
limits: The identicality rule is a modelling choice; re-representation is handled outside the match.
agent_relevance: A usable spec: strict by default, with a documented relaxation path.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett, Gentner (2017) Extending SME to handle large-scale cognitive modeling
finding: Greedy merge replaces exhaustive merge: start with the highest-scoring kernel and add consistent ones, giving polynomial time. It found the same best mapping as exhaustive merge in 52 of 56 analogies. Failures arise when many large kernels conflict with each other.
numbers: 52 of 56 identical (93%); 4 of 56 non-optimal. Non-optimal cases also seen on large diagrams. Grootswagers (2013) explored when greedy is optimal; the authors reject factorial alternatives (van Rooij et al. 2008; Wareham et al. 2011).
limits: The test set was SME's own example library (Forbus and Oblinger 1990), not an independent sample.
agent_relevance: A greedy mapper is enough for agent use. Keep the top 2 or 3 mappings and compare, as the 20% rule does, rather than trust one.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett, Gentner (2017) Extending SME to handle large-scale cognitive modeling
finding: Evidence for SME's local-to-global time course: under a 600 ms deadline people judged directional metaphors ('Some suburbs are parasites' vs 'Some parasites are suburbs') as equally comprehensible; by 1200 ms the forward direction won. This fits an early symmetric alignment, then directional inference.
numbers: Deadlines 600 ms and 1200 ms (Wolff and Gentner 2011).
limits: One lab, one paradigm; mapped to SME by the authors.
agent_relevance: Order of operations: match first, direct the inferences second. Do not infer from a half-built mapping.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett, Gentner (2017) Extending SME to handle large-scale cognitive modeling
finding: Candidate inferences get their own structural score: support (how much matched structure backs the inference, by trickle-down) and extrapolation (how far it goes beyond that support). More support is always better; high extrapolation is wanted in brainstorming but is riskier for prediction.
numbers: Two measures, ratio-based; no accuracy figures in the passage read.
limits: Proposed measures tied to plausibility ratings in cited studies; not independently replicated in what I read.
agent_relevance: Directly usable: score a transferred step by support and flag extrapolation; refuse high-extrapolation steps in routine problems.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett, Gentner (2017) Extending SME to handle large-scale cognitive modeling
finding: Application: SME with CogSketch qualitative visual representations solved most problems in a visual oddity task used with Munduruku and North American groups, and failed on those hardest for people. An ablation (edge-level vs object-level focus) reproduced the group difference.
numbers: 39 of 45 problems solved (87%); failures were among those hardest for human participants.
limits: Single task; representations built by CogSketch from PowerPoint stimuli; the cultural ablation is an interpretation from one model.
agent_relevance: Shows SME works on machine-built representations, which answers part of the hand-coding charge; but the representation builder is the real work.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction
finding: ACME is the main rival. It treats structure (isomorphism), semantic similarity and pragmatic centrality as soft pressures settled in one parallel constraint-satisfaction network, giving one best mapping. It allows non-identical relations to map; SME needs identical relations. Systematicity is handled symmetrically as a special case of using related propositions.
numbers: Run on the Gentner and Toupin stories: correct mapping found in all conditions except the unsystematic cross-mapped one, where the network failed to settle until parameters were changed (inhibition -.2 to -.1, or min -1 to -.3). Lightbulb/radiation problems mapped in about 3 cycles to success.
limits: Compares with SME as of 1986 and calls ACME an extension. Parameters tuned per run. Does not model access.
agent_relevance: Alternative design: soft scoring with relevance weights. Useful if O7 should weight goal-relevant relations, which SME deliberately does not.

source: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: a theory of analogical access and mapping (LISA)
finding: LISA criticises both SME and ACME: they build many local match hypotheses then discard most (not plausible given working memory), map analogies of any size with equal ease, and do not link access to mapping. LISA uses dynamic binding by synchrony, a working-memory limit on how many role bindings are active, and one mechanism for access and mapping.
numbers: No single figure; the claim is that human mapping is limited by the number of simultaneous bindings, which SME and ACME do not capture. Simulates cross-mapping, surface and capacity effects.
quote: these models are too good at analogical mapping
limits: The capacity argument is a theory claim, not a measured test in the passages read.
agent_relevance: Mapping size should be capped. Small bounded mappings (a handful of relations) are closer to what people manage and are cheaper to check.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Markman, Ferguson (1998) Analogy just looks like high level perception
finding: Reply to Chalmers, French and Hofstadter (1992), who charged SME with hand-coded representations and with splitting apart perception and comparison. The reply: SME has been fed representations built by other programs (PHINEAS, MAGI, MARS); inputs hold irrelevant and misleading matches, so the winner is chosen from many; and SME handles very large inputs. It also says PHINEAS builds larger representations than Copycat's problems.
numbers: No effect sizes; tables of relative complexity of Copycat vs PHINEAS domain theories.
limits: Authors replying to their critics; Chalmers et al. 1992 itself was not opened. Hand-coded input remains a real cost.
agent_relevance: The critique is the real risk to O7: if the agent writes the representation itself, the match is steered by it. Use a fixed schema for descriptions and build both sides with the same extractor.

source: Gentner and Markman (1997) on the scope of structure mapping
finding: Boundary of the theory: structure mapping covers the mapping stage only. Access (retrieval) follows surface similarity; evaluation and re-representation are separate. MAC/FAC is the paired retrieval model: a cheap content-vector scan, then SME on the survivors.
numbers: Karla the Hawk results (Gentner et al. 1993) cited: retrieval rises with surface overlap; soundness rises with shared causal structure. Figures are in subfield 03.
limits: Pointer only; numbers are in the 03 files.
agent_relevance: Never expect the mapping step to find the analogue. Retrieval has to be forced to come from relations or from an outside index.
